content: A printed circuit board (PCB) is a structure designed to mechanically support and electrically connect electronic components. This is achieved through conductive pathways, known as traces, which are etched from copper sheets laminated onto a non-conductive substrate. Alternative terms for PCBs include printed wiring boards (PWBs) and etched wiring boards. When electronic components are mounted onto a PCB, it is referred to as a printed circuit assembly (PCA) or printed circuit board assembly (PCBA). PCBs are known for their durability, cost-effectiveness, and reliability, especially in high-volume production. However, their design and initial manufacturing require significant effort and expense compared to wire-wrapped or point-to-point constructed circuits. The design, assembly, and quality control of PCBs are governed by standards established by the IPC organization. Materials The conductive layers of PCBs are typically made from thin copper foil, while the insulating layers are composed of materials such as phenolic paper, glass fiber, or various plastics. A common material used in PCB manufacturing is prepreg, which is a combination of glass fiber mat, nonwoven material, and resin. Copper foil and prepreg are laminated together using epoxy resin. Common prepreg materials include FR-2 (phenolic cotton paper), FR-3 (cotton paper and epoxy), FR-4 (woven glass and epoxy), FR-5 (woven glass and epoxy), FR-6 (matte glass and polyester), G-10 (woven glass and epoxy), and CEM series materials. Patterning (Etching) Most PCBs are manufactured by bonding a layer of copper over the entire substrate, sometimes on both sides, to create a blank PCB. Unwanted copper is then removed using a temporary mask and etching techniques, leaving only the desired copper traces. Alternatively, traces can be added to a bare substrate through electroplating processes. Three common subtractive methods for removing copper include: 1. Silk Screen Printing: Etch-resistant inks are applied to protect the copper foil, and the unwanted copper is removed through etching. Conductive inks can also be printed on non-conductive boards for hybrid circuits. 2. Photoengraving: A photomask and chemical etching are used to remove copper. The photomask is created using computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) software, and laser-printed transparencies or direct laser imaging are employed for high-resolution requirements. 3. PCB Milling: A mechanical milling system removes copper foil from the substrate. The milling machine operates like a plotter, guided by design files in HPGL or Gerber format. Additive processes, such as the semi-additive process, are also used. In this method, a thin copper layer is already present on the board, and additional copper is plated onto unmasked areas. This process is particularly useful for multi-layer boards, as it allows for the creation of conductive vias. Lamination Multi-layer PCBs, which contain internal trace layers, are created by bonding together separately etched thin boards. Drilling Holes, or vias, are drilled into PCBs using tungsten carbide drill bits. Automated drilling machines, guided by computer-generated files (e.g. For very small vias, laser drilling is often used, though it may result in inferior surface finishes. Specialized vias include: Blind Vias: Connect an internal copper layer to an outer layer. Buried Vias: Connect internal copper layers without reaching the outer layers. For multi-layer boards, the walls of the holes are plated with copper to form plated-through holes, which electrically connect the layers. A chemical de-smear or plasma-etch process is used to remove bonding agent residue before plating. Traditional methods include hot air solder leveling (HASL) with tin-lead solder, though lead-free alternatives are now used to comply with RoHS regulations. Other plating options include organic surface protectants (OSP), immersion silver, immersion tin, electroless nickel with immersion gold (ENIG), and direct gold plating. Edge connectors are often gold-plated for durability. Solder Resist A polymer solder resist coating is applied to areas that should not be soldered. This prevents solder bridging between conductors, reducing the risk of short circuits and providing environmental protection. Screen Printing Text and line art can be printed onto the PCB's surface using screen printing. This is used to label component designators, test points, and other assembly or servicing information. Digital printing methods are increasingly replacing traditional screen printing, allowing for variable data such as serialization and barcodes. Testing Unpopulated PCBs undergo bare-board testing to verify circuit connections. High-volume production uses bed-of-nails testers, while smaller volumes may use flying-probe testers. Testing identifies shorts (unwanted connections) and opens (missing connections). Populated boards are tested through: Visual Inspection: Manual or automated optical inspection. Power-Off Testing: Analog signature analysis. In-Circuit Testing: Functional Testing: Verifying the board's intended operation. Boundary scan testing, based on the JTAG standard, is used to test integrated circuits and program nonvolatile memory components. Printed Circuit Assembly After PCB fabrication, electronic components are mounted to create a printed circuit assembly (PCA). Components can be attached using through-hole or surface-mount techniques. Soldering methods include wave soldering, reflow ovens, or manual soldering for prototypes. Some components, such as Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs), require specialized soldering techniques. A combination of through-hole and surface-mount methods is often used to balance strength and space efficiency. Protection and Packaging PCBs for extreme environments are coated with conformal materials like silicone rubber, polyurethane, acrylic, or epoxy to prevent corrosion and short circuits. Assembled PCBs are often stored in antistatic bags to protect against static discharge, which can damage fine traces or components. Safety Certification In the U.S., UL 796 sets safety standards for PCBs, evaluating characteristics such as flammability, operating temperature, and electrical tracking. Cordwood Construction Cordwood construction, used in space-constrained applications like missile systems, involves mounting components axially between parallel planes. Components are connected using nickel tapes welded to their leads. This method allowed high packing densities before the advent of integrated circuits but has largely been replaced by surface-mount technology. Multiwire Boards Multiwire technology embeds machine-routed insulated wires in a non-conductive matrix. This method simplifies design and reduces crosstalk but is cost-prohibitive for large-scale production. Surface-Mount Technology Surface-mount technology (SMT) emerged in the 1960s and became widespread by the 1990s. Components are designed with metal tabs or end caps for direct soldering to the PCB surface. SMT allows for smaller components, higher circuit densities, and automation, reducing labor costs and improving production quality. SMT components are often smaller and cheaper than their through-hole counterparts, though some wire-ended components remain more cost-effective.
